paragraphs: Blue sky and historic buildings. Cherry blossoms here and there, and people on terrace seats enjoying beer and music. That was the kind of city Munich was, where I spent five weeks. Contrary to the refreshing and warm streets, my heart was unusually shaken when I first stepped off at Munich Central Station. On the first day of my study abroad, the city's public transport was mostly cancelled because of a strike. And my SIM card, for some reason, stopped being able to communicate once I entered Germany. But at the same time, I remember being very excited. "Since such an incident happened on the first day, nothing worse can happen. It will surely be a good study abroad."

The University of Munich is named after a Bavarian king and is called Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München (LMU) in German. It is also the university where Roentgen, who discovered X-rays, conducted research. The medical school campuses are one near the central station and one at Großhadern, away from the city, and I mainly did my clerkship at the latter. The clerkship at LMU is a little different from clerkships at other universities, and for the first three weeks I took part in the Winter School hosted by the university. The Winter School is held in the Neurology Department and the Oncology Department, and I took part in the Neurology Winter School. About 30 students took part in this Winter School, half of them LMU students and the rest students who had gathered from around the world, starting with Europe, such as Brazil, Mexico, India and Tanzania. Each exchange student was paired with an LMU student and did the clerkship on the same ward. My study buddy was a fifth-year female student, kind and strongly responsible.

The morning in Neurology starts at 8 o'clock. First I changed into large scrubs and drew blood from inpatients. LMU students are like Japanese residents: they can do everything themselves, from blood drawing and line placement to bold lumbar punctures without local anesthesia. The patients were cooperative too, and nobody refused medical procedures by students. When I failed at a blood draw, the warm words "Learning by doing!" with which they allowed me to try again remain in my heart even now. After blood drawing, we made ward rounds by the students and residents. On the ward where I trained there were more than ten patients with brain tumours, infections, neuroimmunological diseases and so on. Rounds were in German, but my study buddy explained the key points in English, so talking with the resident about cases and asking questions was not that difficult. After rounds, the students did the interviews and neurological examinations of newly admitted patients and reported the content to the resident. We divided the examinations with my study buddy, and for patients who could not speak English she also interpreted for me. Besides this, there was a case report meeting for the whole Neurology Department twice a week and rounds by the Chief Professor once a week.

After having lunch in the canteen, I took part in the radiologic conference or chatted with friends over coffee at the cafe. The afternoon clerkship was mainly classroom learning. The content was lectures on neurological diseases in general, such as cerebral infarction, neurodegenerative diseases and epilepsy, a visit to a pediatric neurology hospital, case discussions and so on. In the lectures I was able to learn widely about content that followed diagnosis in clinical practice, about basic research, and about the mechanism of fMRI. Also, when I visited a rehabilitation hospital, I tried an exoskeleton robot and a game-style treadmill.

For the latter two weeks, I was allowed to train in the neurodegenerative disease outpatient clinic. Also, since I was interested in hematology as well as neurology, I was able to have a friend at LMU who does leukemia research show me the laboratory. The outpatient clinic of the neurodegenerative disease group was divided into a movement disorder clinic and a dementia clinic, and I rotated one week through each. In the movement disorder clinic, besides seeing patients with Parkinson's disease, multiple system atrophy, progressive supranuclear palsy, corticobasal syndrome, Huntington's disease and essential tremor, I also observed botulinum therapy for cervical dystonia. Corticobasal syndrome is quite a rare disease, and being able to actually see an alien hand was a valuable experience. The patients in the dementia clinic were mainly Alzheimer's dementia and dementia with Lewy bodies, but I could also see follow-up of Down syndrome and neuropsychological tests. Of course, practice in the outpatient clinic was conducted in German, and I felt frustrated at having to be given an explanation in English each time and at not being able to say a single word to a patient who had started crying. However, when learning neurological cases, the existence of a language barrier is not entirely bad. Precisely because I could not understand the words, I could concentrate on the physical findings important for diagnosis and on the patients' emotional movements. Now I can proudly say that, thanks to this study abroad experience, I have become able to observe patients well.

During the Winter School, a room in a student dormitory in Olympia Park was provided. It had a bed, desk, kitchen and tableware, toilet and shower room, all included, and the room was reasonably clean. On the grounds there were a supermarket, bakery, bar, ATM, post office and coin laundry, and I had no particular trouble living there. After leaving the dormitory I moved to a room I found on Airbnb, where I was also able to stay comfortably.

Because I did not want to waste a single day during the study abroad, after clerkship on weekdays I went to eat with friends, went to art museums and ballet performances, and compared beers and sausages. On days off I took part in the Winter School recreation or took day trips to the suburbs by myself. Students of Oncology as well as Neurology took part in the recreation, and we were able to deepen friendships. Being able to touch history and art in an environment where they are close at hand refreshed me even during the clerkship.

In Munich I was also able to meet the LMU students who had taken part together with me in the LMU-NU Collaborative Online USMLE Review Classes. They had given me advice on various matters since before I left, and locally they showed me around the city. When students from Nagoya University who were studying at other European universities visited Munich on a weekend, we ate together.

During the five weeks of study abroad, what I kept in mind were the words Dr. 坂野 said at the pre-departure training. "Do your very best with what you can do." At first I interpreted it as being about ability in the clerkship. And, as expected, I keenly felt how low my English ability was. At that time, my study buddy said this to me. "You are always positive. You always say 'Yes! I want to do it!'." What I can do. That is to do the clerkship seriously every day, to keep time, and to always be a positive yes-man. Ability is certainly necessary. But more than that, I think that it is one's attitude that makes one's evaluation. Finally, I would like to thank everyone who supported this study abroad.
